Crushing Jaws in Neutral is even worse than Clever. It has less hitboxes, is extremely slow, and very reactable. Still, its only redeeming quality is the fact that [i]Crushing Jaws[/i]' second hit is unblockable. So there is a chance that against an opponent who lacks some form of intelligence, it can land in Neutral and net Locust Guy a combo for free. The more practical usage is to use this skill on wakeup. There's 2 ways to do it: [b]Time and Land the first hit[/b]: On success, this would let [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] deal its full damage and continue Locust Guy's Combo. However, it is very precise and very unforgiving. Notes: Black Mucus's ragdoll time can set up a pretty favorable scenario where Locust Guy can perform this consistently, but it is still, again, very precise and unforgiving. [b]Miss the first hit and Land the second hit[/b]: This version is a lot less strict and precise thanks to the second hit being unblockable. But Locust Guy would lose out 4 damage from doing this. First Version Second Version

A relatively low risk, mid reward mixup that every Locust Guy can afford to do every time as they wish. The basic idea is: ... Air Combo M1 ... (Hold Block) Air Stun ends ... (Hold Block) ... Shortened DSL ... R M1 ... (Hold F) R ends ... (Hold F) ... [i]What?[/i] To explain it in plain word, Locust Guy would want to do an [url=#sec-air-combo]Air Combo[/url], hit an M1, and then just hold Block until both characters start falling down. This enables a few paths for Locust Guy to take: [b]Front Dash[/b]: Thanks to the fact that Locust Guy starts falling down first instead of the opponent and Front Dash ragdoll vertical check isn't that high, if Locust Guy lands this Front Dash, it will be a completely free M1 reset. [b]Block and Perfect M1[/b]: The second option is to Block the opponent counter M1 when they are falling down. Depending on the matchup, the opponent M1 block endlag could be more than 16f, which means Locust Guy can punish it right after with his 14f startup M1s. This, of course, leads into an M1 reset. [b]Side Dash around[/b]: The final option is to Side Dash around the opponent. It can be 180 dash, 360 dash or whatever, this last option creates a pseudo-forced M1 trade right after an Air Combo. There is one glaring issue with this mixup. It is that the opponent can just usually side dash away from it once the Air Combo stun ends, so this is best used when the opponent least expected it

Having no effective Neutral abilities, Locust Guy is bound to be hard countered by any character with superior Neutral game. But it isn't as hopeless as it seems (it is still pretty hopeless regardless). Locust Guy still has some tricks to get around some of the most oppresive neutral in the game, and it has to do with [url=#sec-fluttering-pounce]Fluttering Pounce[/url]. [b]"Fly over it"[/b] is a popular way to use the R special. Basically, Locust Guy can fly over quite a few things in this game such as Blood Manipulator's Supernova, Puppet Master's Heat Emission, Disaster Plants' Root Swarm, and more. After avoiding the attack, Locust Guy can come down and roll into the opponent, instantly initiating an M1 trade. [b]Fluttering Jumpscare[/b] is another way that Locust Guy can employ to deal with other characters' Neutral game. The idea is to fly straight into the opponent when they are thinking about how to approach the Locust Guy with their Neutral options. Nine times out of ten, if done correctly, Locust Guy can often catch these opponent by surprise, stopping the opponent's offense and starting a combo. [b]Black Mucus[/b] is a blockbreaking projectile with a decent hitbox size. It ragdolls on hit, which means it can threaten things like Ten Shadows' Divine Dog or Black Death's Earthen Insect Trance. Mentioned earlier, the opponent could choose to burn their sidedash to dodge this attack, which means that Locust Guy now have an advantage to dash in with his own Sidedash M1 and win the engagement. It functions like a microscopic version of Aspiring Mangaka's Clairvoyance, which is to disable the opponent sidedash, giving the attacker the upper hand in engaging and winning that engagement. Upon using [i]Clever[/i], Locust Guy throws out a barrage of punches using two of his arms (not four). This attack has multiple continous hitbox, around 14 of them in total; They would together deal 14.2 damage. This skill has a fairly decent startup of 24f with a pretty quick and semi-unpunishable recovery of 15f. However, this skill has a great amount of block endlag of 43f, so it is not recommended to use this skill in Neutral as it can be easily blocked. On hit, Locust Guy gain a +28f advantage over the standing stunned opponent; this advantage can chain to pretty much anything in Locust Guy kit beside [i]Black Mucus[/i].

[i]Clever[/i] is mainly used as a combo extender used in between M1 chains to deal extra damage, however as it does not lead into a full M1 reset like Shut Up! (Aspiring Mangaka), or even an M1 Rewind like Shutter Door or Focus Strike (Restless Gambler and Perfection), but continues where Locust Guy left off. This is due to its M1 remembrance mechanic, where it remembers your last M1 for around a second. This mechanic is also why doing 4 M1s into Clever often leaves Locust Guy unable to M1 for a longer time than usual. Despite being unable to hit ragdoll, Clever can hit aerial ragdoll, meaning if Locust Guy knows his opponent doesn't have evasive, he can get extra damage by using uppercut into Clever, however after Clever Locust Guy are unable to M1 until his opponent is actionable, leaving his only viable moves as [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] and [i]Wing Throw[/i]. There exists a Tech for [i]Clever[/i] that can be considered the kind of viable: Clever can lead to an extra M1 if Clever is used after the first (and only the first) M1, which is called [url=#sec-m1s-farm]Clever Extra M1[/url] There is also another notable Tech that ends an air combo with a [i]Clever[/i]: [url=#sec-m1s-farm]Clever Slam[/url]; this is a great tech as it lets Locust Guy get in an extra Downslam during his combo, or lead into another evasive bait combo thanks to Clever restanding the opponent. Basically, [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] and [i]Wing Throw[/i] are both an option after [i]Clever[/i], instead of just [i]Wing Throw[/i] after a Downslam from an air combo

Locust Guy winds up his head backwards to spew out [i]Black Mucus[/i] at the enemy with a startup of 35f and a recovery of 22f, giving Locust Guy a +28f advantage with the attack being unlockable. Upon landing the hit, the enemy receives a debuff that gives Locust Guy a 15% damage reduction for 13 seconds. [i]Black Mucus[/i] travels for about 57 studs. The debuff effect for this move can be stacked exponentially, though only if you have other Locust Guy; after 7-8 hits, the opponent starts healing Locust Guy by trying to deal damage to him since the damage reduction goes above 100%.

The strategy for this move is similar to other projectiles like [i]Bud Shot[/i] or [i]Soul Fire[/i], mainly used as a mix up zoning/interrupting tool due to it being unblockable and having relatively fast travel speed. Due to its relatively big startup, it is not recommended to just throw it out in neutral, unless it is used to bait their side dash. Locust Guy can use [i]Black Mucus[/i] to make [i]Crushing Jaws getup[/i] easier Because [i]Black Mucus[/i] applies a flat 15% damage reduction to all moves, Locust Guy can survive attacks that would normally kill them ([i]Head Splitter[/i], [i]Plasma Wave[/i]) if the enemy has the debuff applied

Locust Guy winds up his head backwards to bite the opponent with a startup of 24f. Then, after 24 inactive frames takes a second bite, and finally, after 26 inactive frames, a third bite. This makes Locust Guy drag the opponent through the floor, and after 171 inactive frames, Locust Guy slams the opponent into the ground. This makes them bounce back into the air, allowing for an [i]Air Combo[/i] opportunity even if [i]Fluttering Pounce[/i] is off cooldown. The opponent takes a recovery of 102f to get up from the slam. The first bite of [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] is blockable, though it does not stop the second attack from initiating, rather making it 40% slower also applying to the third bite, increasing their inactive frames to 40f and 43f. The total damage of this move is 16 dealing 4 damage for each part. During the windup for the slam, Locust Guy gets complete I-frames.

This moves main strategy is using it as a cooldown staller because of its extremely long target stun of 351f or, alternatively, as a combo extender for [i]Clever[/i] since it makes up the best true combo in Locust Guy's kit. [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] can be used as a risky mixup, though it is not recommended since the [multicolor=#a3e635,#15803d]Clever mixup[/multicolor] is much better and safer. This move is the most punishable part of Locust Guy's kit, since it allows the enemy to evasive punish if done correctly, or as an alternative, the opponent can use a move such as [i]Rough Energy[/i] to surprise Locust Guy. Because of the complete I-frames that Locust Guy gets during his inactive frames leading up for the slam, [i]Crushing Jaws[/i] is by far the best base move in his kit to deal with domains, since it allows him to stall for more time while also being invincible to any damage the domain is inflicting on him.

Upon using the move, Locust Guy grabs the opponent into the air and throws them shortly after, allowing for an [i]Air Combo[/i] even if [i]Fluttering Pounce[/i] is on cooldown. Wing Throw has an average for Locust Guy startup of 24f but a very long block endlag of 42f if blocked. It can bypass ragdoll and has a relatively short cooldown which makes it the best combo extender in Locust Guy's kit.

The main strategy for this move should be using it as a combo extender off ragdoll, as it allows Locust Guy to combo into [i]Clever[/i] or [i]Crushing Jaws[/i]. This move should not be used as a neutral option, since it's blockable and has an average startup for Locust Guy and a very long block endlag. By aiming [i]Wing Throw[/i] upwards you can catch the opponent with [i]Clever[/i] performing the "[i][url=#sec-classic-tech-table]Clever Clever[/url][/i]" tech or catching them with an M1 perfoming an "[i][url=#sec-classic-tech-table]RSA[/url][/i]". Note that "[url=#sec-classic-tech-table]Clever Clever[/url]" tech is much easier to do than [url=#sec-classic-tech-table]RSA[/url], so even if going for this high risk strategy, you should use "[url=#sec-classic-tech-table]Clever Clever[/url]" tech since "[url=#sec-classic-tech-table]RSA[/url]" can only offer an extra M1.

Locust Guy travels forward while flapping his wings for 21f. They can go into any direction by aiming their camera. [i]Fluttering Pounce[/i] can be cancelled early by pressing M1. This move has a cooldown of 16s.

[i]Fluttering Pounce[/i] can be used as a mixup option acting as a pseudo-dash, due to its high travelling speed and a relatively quiet audio cue. Aiming [i]Fluttering Pounce[/i] upwards is also a great mixup option, as it grants Locust Guy vertical mobility. This lets him dodge moves such as [i]Cleaving Whirlwind[/i] and then frontdash down onto the enemy or roll to confuse the opponent even further. By timing Fluttering Pounce correctly, you can land an extra M1 resulting in a group of tech known as [url=#sec-poor-man-s-umbilical]Poor Man's Umbilical[/url].

Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant is Locust Guy's main (only) gimmick and combo extender, and is a core part of his kit. Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant can be used after and uppercut surf for increased damage. If timed correctly, an M1 can be used once before using Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant in order to do 3 M1s in the air instead of the regular 2 M1s (and is used in the "Heavy Combo" Mentioned by the Overview.

This tech is used to do a complete M1 reset using just Wing Throw, maximising damage and such ... Wing Throw (Aim up) M1 (x3, catch) ... Shortened DSL ... 4 (Aim up) M1 (x3, catch) ... Perhaps one of Locust Guy hardest Tech, this tech will allow an M1 reset if pulled off successfully. But there are [b]FOUR[/b] major roadblocks that stop this Tech from being consistent and easy to perform: Map, Ragdoll Physics, Directional Influence (DI), and Evasive [i]Map[/i]: This Tech is basically impossible to pull off in a map with a low ceiling as Locust Guy needs to fly up to max height and throw the opponent at the apex of Wing Throw [i]Ragdoll Physics[/i]: Ragdoll in JJS interact really weirdly with Wing Throw, and Locust Guy can't control it. Sometimes the opponent body would clip into Locust Guy during the move, making throwing the opponent straight up basically impossible [i]Directional Influence (DI)[/i]: One of the more niche and less known mechanics in JJS, A player can hold down W/A/S/D to change the flying path direction of their Air Ragdoll ever so slightly. This mechanic is majorly present in Disaster Plants counterplay, but it appears here to screw up the Tech anyway (the opponent can just influence their flying direction and make Locust Guy miss his M1s) [i]Evasive[/i]: This Tech require the opponent to have no evasive

[b]First[/b], Locust Guy needs to waste their opponent evasive while not using Wing Throw, so landing a Crushing Jaws would be ideal. [b]Second[/b], Locust Guy needs to land another M1 in another M1 trade to start this. [b]Third[/b], Locust Guy needs to predict where his opponent will land (due to DI), and times his M1s in order to catch them in the air within a margin of error of 0.7s or 42f (He will also has to account for ping difference and input latency. A ping diff too big and this Tech is simply not doable) [b]Fourth[/b], Congratulations!!! Locust Guy has just landed one of his hardest Tech and deal major damage
How to pull this off successfully

The ultimate Tech to majorly mixup people Clever ... Shortened DSL 1 ... :dumbassdog: Despite being easy to perform, this Tech is very risky to do. Locust Guy has plenty of other good options and mixup anyway. Still the aura is simply unmatched. Serious Note Enter the most scariest Locust Guy Tech, the most infamous mixup, The Clever Mixup :aaaaaaaaaa: (screams in fear) Clever Mixup is a Tech in which Locust Guy throws out Clever in Neutral for no apparent reason. Why? Well because it will land on the opponent and net Locust Guy a completely free combo. Of course there's the risk of getting Clever blocked and punished, but that's not the way one uses the Clever Mixup.

Upon use of the [i]Ultimate[/i], Locust Guy extends his abdomen to deal a powerful sting to the opponent. The move has a relatively big startup compared to his base moves of 30f and a pretty long recovery of 33f, this gives Locust Guy a +42f advantage. The move deals 9 damage per second, resulting in 90 damage in total.

The main strategy for this move should be using it after [i]Clever[/i] to guarantee a kill. Depending on the character, [i]Directed Poison[/i] can kill them after just an M1 string (Vessel, Puppet Master). Due to its startup of 30f, the opponent can jump over the [i]Ultimate[/i] to avoid the damage, which is why it's recommended to use it in an [i]Air Combo[/i], since the opponent is stuck in place for about 60f-more than enough to guarantee a hit. It is not recommended using the [i]Ultimate[/i] without first catching the opponent in an M1 string or [i]Clever[/i] because of its big startup and an audio cue alerting the opponent that the attack is coming. The move provides a lot of I-frames which lets you avoid/punish attacks such as Open, acting as a [i]pseudo-counter[/i]. Domains that make the opponent stand in place and dont give them I-frames such as [i]Malevolent Shrine[/i] give Locust Guy a safe opportunity to hit their [i]Ultimate[/i]. It is best to follow up [i]Directed Poison[/i] with either [i]Black Mucus[/i], [i]Wing Throw[/i] or [i]Crushing jaws getup[/i] because of its true ragdoll to guarantee a kill even further.
Lucky Coward drives the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] forward, stabbing the opponent before kicking them away. This puts him and his victim in a short grab animation.

One of the more unique Neutral M1s in the game. Lucky Coward trades less ragdoll time for 1 more damage than other Neutral M1s in the game. This lessened ragdoll time is caused by the very short grab animation on Hit, but it opens up a lots of new strategies: Being even more commital on Follow-ups: Some Skills now need immediate input to be connected after hitting the stab (Side Dash Trip, Cheap Shot or Front Dash); otherwise, the opponent will wake up in time and block the follow up. This plays heavily into Lucky Coward's high committal gameplan. Riding Ragdoll: Holding Space and W (Jump and Moving Forward) when the M1 lands will sometimes let Lucky Coward ride the ragdoll as it gets knocked away. This can let Lucky Coward connect Trip without a Side Dash or start a get-up theory M1 trade immediately without a Side Dash. Ragdoll Manipulation: (I actually don't know much about this, but if someone can expand please help) 1 more damage: It is 1 more damage, who is complaining about 1 more damage?
Lucky Coward swing his Hand Sword up diagonally from right to left, dealing 4 damage and flinging the enemy upward.

This Uppercut is just like every other Uppercuts in the game. It is recommended to learn Uppercut Surfing to do combos with Lucky Coward; combo routes such as Trip on Air Ragdoll knock the opponent away, which can be crucial to Lucky Coward positioning Uppercut (Surf) Trip Saucy Uppercut (Surf) Backstab Lucky Coward can also attempt to farm Miracle using an Uppercut: 1 Miracle on success, but it is pretty risky compared to other Miracle farming methods. Uppercut (Surf) Roll Away R (Drop) Taunt (Back Dash simultaneously)
Lucky Coward grips his sword with both hands and drives it down into the opponent below, pinning them to the floor and dealing 4 damage.
This is a generic Downslam just like every other Downslams in the game. There is nothing too notable about this Move
Following the second swing, Lucky Coward spin his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] to perform a third horizontal swing from left to right, dealing 4 damage.
This is the third M1 in Lucky Coward Basic Attack string. It serves as generic damage just like every other M1s in his kit, but its safety is still something of note.
Lucky Coward swings his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Sword[/color] from right to left, following the first swing and dealing 3 damage.

This M1 is Unpunishable on Block, making it a great tool in winning M1 trades. Lucky Coward can miss the first M1 and time this M1 to hit on the opponent wake up, in order to perform a safe get-up theory M1 trade, compared to using the first M1 on wake up.
Lucky Coward slices horizontally with his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] from left to right, dealing 3 damage.

This M1 has a 16f of Punish window. Enough to be punished by high level players who are using characters with 12f [noauto]startup[/noauto] M1s, but not enough to be consistently punished by those with 13-14f [noauto]startup[/noauto] M1s. This move is best used on wake up, and not recommended to use against fast M1 characters.

Lucky Coward raise his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Sword[/color] up and slice down diagonally from left to right, dealing 12 damage and breaking Block. He can also gain 1 [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Miracle[/color] if he interrupts an opponent action with this Skill. This Skill has a rather quick startup and a really long Lingering Active Hitbox, with minimum Recovery on Whiff/Hit/Block. It can also be perfect blocked.
This Skill is similar to its Grounded variant in every way, except that it moves Lucky Coward forward, covering a decent amount of distance in a short time.

Upon using the skill, Lucky Coward command his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] to do a sweeping attack, cutting their opponent ankles and dealing 10 damage, hence the name. This Skill is really fast, uncancellable even when Lucky Coward is stunned or ragdolled, and can combo into everything. It is one of the main piece in Lucky Coward gameplan and his way of navigating the Neutral State of a fight. However, this Skill has a really low vertical Hitbox, so it can be jumped over.

When used, Lucky Coward drives his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Sword[/color] down to the ragdolled opponent in front of him, pinning them down and dealing 10 damage. If it lands, it will inflict True Ragdoll on the opponent and keep them down for a long time. Like every other Lucky Coward skills so far, it is fast and simple.

A follow-up barrage of attacks to Stinger, Lucky Coward repeatedly thrusts his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Sword[/color] down on the ragdolled opponent in front of him 3 times before stopping, each thrust is unblockable and deal 2 damage for a total of 6 damage. The skill gives Lucky Coward a very short window of time to act before the opponent (Only enough to block). it is important to be cautious when using this move, as the opponent may attempt a reversal.

Due to the incredibly low stun time on behalf of the opponent, the move often leads to a 'scramble situation', where both the Lucky Coward and the opponent can act at the same time in very close proximity. This situation is very slightly in favour of the Lucky Coward, as they can act before the opponent. The Lucky Coward should be wary of oncoming M1s, as the opponent, having just come out of ragdoll, will not be affected by the Lucky Coward's M1s. Some examples of follow-ups for the Lucky Coward: - Side dash -> Backstab - Block to predict an M1 - Drop sword and dodge - Jump on the opponent's head Because of this move's high damage, it could also be viable to simply reset to neutral, as the slight amount of stun the move inflicts allows the Lucky Coward to safely dash away.

Lucky Coward thursts his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] forward, stabbing the opponent and dealing 8 damage. This Skill is fast and an effective blockbreaker/mixup tool. If Lucky Coward hits the front side of the opponent, he will reset his M1s but both sides will get out of stun at roughly the same time. If he hits it in the back side of the opponent, he will not reset his M1s but the opponent is stunned for a longer amount of time.

Lucky Coward command his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] to perform a circular slash up high into the air, dealing 12 damage and ragdolling the opponent for a really long time. The Attack is fast, uncancellable, and can be used in stun/ragdoll just like its brother Ankle Cutter; However, this move trades horizontal hitbox for a really good vertical hitbox instead. Due to how the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] move and position within the environment and its hitbox, this move might not be as good as its brother when it comes to getting Lucky Coward out of problem.

Lucky Coward perform a low kick forward, aiming to trip their opponent and make the fall down. The attack is nearly identical to an M1 in terms of startup and recovery frame data. When used on an ragdolled opponent, this move will kick them away instead. Note that it is the only move that can be used in both Sword On and Sword Off Modes.

Upon using the skill, Lucky Coward throws his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] forward, switching from Sword On to Sword Off. His [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] fly forward while spinning, slicing any opponent in the way and dealing 7 damage. Notably, the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] targetting system will automatically lock on the last target it hits, so it could potentially hit no one and just stand still in a place unless Helping Hand is used.

Lucky Coward waves his right hand, signalling the Hand Sword to fly back to him. After a short startup, the Hand Sword will begin flying back to its owner; at this point it can not be stopped and will return at all cost (to the point of flying through domain barrier or more). The skill deals 8 damage switches Lucky Coward back to Sword On Mode. Notably, this skill do not share cooldown with Cheap Shot, unlike the first and second skills.

While aiming at the enemy and pressing R, Lucky Coward releases his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color], which lets it track and move toward the target. The Hand Sword will always try to go behind the target’s back. This action is completely free and instantanous. While not aiming at anyone and pressing R while [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] is already tracking someone, Lucky Coward will recall the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] to him. The [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] cannot be picked up if he is in Stun or Ragdolled. This action creates a small amount of Self Stun, opening a small window of vulnerability.

Upon Activation, Lucky Coward gain a small 0.25s window to dodge an incoming attack. If successful, he gains a small amount of Melee I-Frames & Bullet I-Frames, denies the attack, and puts the dodge on a 0.15s cooldown. If whiffed, the dodge would be put on a 1s cooldown instead

While looking at a standing target and pressing M1, Lucky Coward start taunting the target, cued by a clown sound effect. After 1.5s of taunting without interruption, Lucky Coward gains 1 [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Miracle[/color], but the Taunt itself lasts 2s total. Furthermore, Lucky Coward will not gain a Miracle if the target is still ragdolled after the 1.5s window of taunting.

Combos' Damage do not account for passive regeneration The Damage of each skill was calculated using the damage modifier in Private Server, the exact method is explained in Writing Guide The difficulty is ranked on a scale of 1 to 8 (Very Easy to Demon Time) Some chains are ping-dependent such as Trip into Front Dash or Trip into Cheap Shot

This is mainly a Sword Off mode thing, a phase in a fight. This phase will not last long however as both players will eventually do something to break the state and try to gain an advantage. Lucky Coward's kit is built to win him this type of engagement. [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] [b]Super Jump[/b]: When picking up or dropping [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color], Lucky Coward can hold down Space and Jump higher than usual. It is not exactly useful everywhere, but it has its niche use cases (Actually I don't know if this is patched or not, anyone please tell me) - This tech still works, it can be used to gain a roll for extra mobility.

Quickly gaining 3 Miracles off of one Front Dash Front Dash (On ragdoll) Taunt Shuffling High Time Back Dash Taunt Shuffling Ankle Cutter Taunt Dirty Play/Helping Hand (Recall)
Main theories/concepts being used for Lucky Coward: Get-up Theory: Hitting on opponent wake up Advanced Positioning Movestacking

Lucky Coward is not a particularly "techy" character perchance. But when it comes to applying some of the technical theory, he is quite consistent at it. This is due to how simple his moves synergize with each others. For example, using Backstab on wake up is a common tech that help getting Lucky Coward a combo on the opponent wake up, and it is simple and consistent enough to do it over and over again. Other more important part of his technical gameplan is to learn how to position himself and his [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] for the best result and the correct way to stack moves on top of each other to apply pressure, or deal quick technically unevasivable damage. Positioning is extra important to Lucky Coward survival and overall gameplan. Due to how destruction just straight up screws with the Hand Sword pathfinding, learning to pay attention to the Sword and making the right decision while also placing yourself at the ideal spot will turn a regular Lucky Coward into a high level one. When you have played Lucky Coward for a long time and is playing him in this current version (1.81.2). You will know that Destruction is re-enabled in ranked. This is rather bad news for Lucky Coward, so here's a list of stupid fuckery that can happen to him: - Hand Sword deciding to move 100 studs away from the opponent. - Hand Sword staying still in a no debris spot because apparently 1 stud height is enough to break the pathfinding. - Hand Sword's attacks spin uncontrollably and miss when used under debris/unbreakable parts of the map. - Ankle Cutter would miss if the opponent is 1 stud below/above thanks to the debris - Ankle Cutter would miss if there is debris in the way because it makes the Sword changes it attack direction or straight up blocks it. - Cheap Shot missing due to opponent lying on broken floor because the attack does reach 1 stud below. - Debris blocking your cursor so you can't redirect/recall the Hand Sword. - Hand Sword taking its stroll through the National Park before coming back to you. Vessel tends to be a very easy matchup for Lucky Coward. In neutral, they dont really have any options against Ankle Cutter, except a well timed 1r or 2r, but it's very unreliable to dodge this way. They're just an M1 merchant and you can easily read or react to their aggressive dashes and dodge + trip/dash. About dodging, all of their moves are dodgable and the dash moves have very telegraphed startups. In case of Vessel landing an M1, their options aren't good, their best bet is to use normal Cursed Strikes as quickly as possible to give themselves i-frames and hopefully make you whiff a move, but even then, this move is punishable after it ends by either Ankle Cutter or High Time (this one less consistent), the Aerial version is also punishable by these moves. Crushing Blow surprisingly doesn't give the Vessel i-frames and can be easily punished mid-move. Black Flash is punishable with evasive into Trip, and Black Flash chaining punished by Ankle Cutter. Counters aren't good against Lucky Coward since the sword counts as an NPC and therefor Manji Kick will counter the air in case of Ankle Cutter and High Time hitting. This is not the case for Dirty Play and Cheap Shot, so keep that in mind.

This matchup is very awkward. The main reason is that Ten Shadows can just feed you to the rabbits and unable your dash when you're sword-off and hold block to either make you take 14 free damage or make you use Dirty Play (sword will probably not come in time) to reduce slightly the damage, pretty bad since it's one of your best neutral tools. Then there's Toad, which is also guaranteed to land if you're sword-off but at least this move is punishable on hit by an Ankle Cutter or High Time. And lastly, Divine Dogs, which you can react and dodge, but if Ten Shadows gets upclose to add more pressure with m1s, it becomes really hard to keep up with the tempo. There's still some room for counterplay, you can cancel Rabbit Escape, manage your cooldowns to never get forced into a combo by Toad, and Trip or use any ragdoll move against Divine Dogs (you can also play sword-on, but you're just an m1 trading vegetable against a better m1 trading character). It's a tricky matchup but playable and winnable.

A very tough encounter for Lucky Coward. Supernova creates an extreme disadvantage since it's an "Explosion" type move, and Lucky Coward can only dodge "Melee" and "Bullet" moves. It forces you to use sword mode in its positioning. Ankle Cutter and High Time can be used to prevent Blood Manipulator playing off supernova however, and can be used to prevent a build up and run off a combo from hit. Talking about other moves, Piercing Blood is undodgable (as it does not count as "Melee" or "Bullet"), which makes it a threat in neutral. However Piercing Blood can be punished for its use due to its end-lag - allowing Ankle Cutter or High Time to punish. Flowing Red Scale's aerial counterpart can help avoid Ankle Cutter, although High Time can punish it. Flowing Red Scale's variants can be dodged by Haruta. Blood Edge can be dodged in all hits. It should be noted Supernova can counter Hand Sword due to it being melee. Flowing Red Scale, Blood Edge and Supernova counter provide iframes during their attack, but leave them open during start up and after.

Defense Attorney moves create pressure with its block breaks and move interrupts. R+1 can be very oppressive against other characters, but Lucky Coward can ignore the play as it deals no damage to non-block, and can punish immediately with sword - which does not count as a move interrupt by Defense Attorney. 1 can be difficult to dodge due to it being a multi-hit and it does give IFrames in the middle of the move, however it can be punished directly after the final hit. 2 is easy to dodge and punish due to its long wind up. While 3+R or 3+3 does bypass Lucky Coward's dodge, it is punishable for using due to end lag and due to the fact it does have a thin hitbox and can be dashed out of. Usually, it can be dodged and leaves Defense Attorney very open for a punish. Aerial 3 can be dodged. Defense Attorney's 4 game can be completely ignored with Lucky Coward. 4's first and second hit are dodgable, and so is 4+R. Additionally, it doesn't provide IFrames allowing for punishplay. 4 into 1 can be ignore as there is no need to block if you can dodge.

Puppet Master heavily suppresses Swordless Lucky Coward's neutral through Ultra Cannon and Heat Emission, forcing him to spend evasive with little value or risk taking substantial damage from Offload puppets. Although Lucky Coward can dodge puppets to generate Miracles in neutral, this is inconsistent because Puppet Master can close the gap and force an M1 interaction or use another move before Lucky Coward can safely capitalize. Swordless Lucky Coward also struggles to disable Puppet Master's puppets due to their unpredictable positioning. Puppet Master's combos are generally safe from swordless interruptions because his moves grant I-frames on hit or the puppets themselves perform the combo with I-frames. Miracle evasive can shut down some of Puppet Master's more dangerous combo routes, but it often provides little value against safer routes that still deal substantial damage to Lucky Coward's fragile health while draining his Miracles. Puppet Master also outdamages Lucky Coward, even if Lucky Coward lands all of his green combos. With safer neutral options and answers to Lucky Coward's approaches in both Sword and Swordless states, Puppet Master can dictate the pace of the matchup and steadily overwhelm him.

Salaryman's moves focus on mind games, punishing heavily for blocking or attacking with Ratio. Lucky Coward is able to avoid these interactions by simply dodging. Every move of Salaryman is dodgable due to being a melee, meaning you can avoid the punishing block-breaks Salaryman uses.

Disaster Plants has a strong advantage against Lucky Coward because many of Disaster Plants' options, including R + 2 and Front Dash, bypass Dodge. This significantly limits Lucky Coward's ability to rely on his usual swordless defensive gameplan. Disaster Plants can also continue playing her bread-and-butter strategy of baiting dashes, which Lucky Coward has no consistent way to circumvent. This gets worse as Lucky Coward's primary Miracle farming is heavily scrutinized because Bud Shots and R + 2 can negate Taunt setups, while her Uppercut M1 being deceptively long-ranged, making Dodge even more restricted than it already was. However, Lucky Coward still has some counterplay, albeit reliant on Disaster Plants' mistakes. The long active duration of Disaster Plants' Front Dash, Aerial Defense Response, and Surging Thorns allows Swordless Lucky Coward to threaten interruptions and potentially start a combo or bait evasive. The main issue is that Lucky Coward must identify mistakes in Disaster Plants' positioning and move timing to exploit these openings. If he fails to do so or she simply plays optimally, Disaster Plants can repeatedly use Aerial Defense Response (which she is encouraged to naturally do against Lucky Coward) to stack spikes around the map, turning even small mistakes into significant backloaded damage and gradually draining Lucky Coward's health and Miracles. Despite the odds, Lucky Coward must make Disaster Plants more hesitant in neutral and needs to deal as much damage as possible before she recovers her full moveset and resumes passively stacking spikes. If the fight becomes a prolonged war of attrition, Disaster Plants' ability to control the map and punish Lucky Coward's restricted options gives her a dominating advantage.

Register's neutral tools naturally bypass Lucky Coward's Dodge. Register can stall and cycle cooldowns with Littering, close the gap with Pole Vault, poke with Garage Sale or Gushing Wound, and secure a combo or bait evasive with Red Seal Speed Crash. These options are generally safe and allow Register to maintain neutral pressure. However, Register's evasive baits are comparatively limited, and many of his high-damage combos, such as Uppercut Homerun and Blunt Trauma, are highly punishable by Miracle evasive. This can significantly restrict his damage output when Lucky Coward manages his resources optimally. But, Lucky Coward can switch between Sword and Swordless modes based on Register's cooldowns and available options, allowing him to interrupt many of Register's pokes and combos with Ankle Cutter and generate Miracles at the sametime. He also has higher damage potential, stronger evasive baits, and more combo opportunities through swordless moves. All in all, this is an even matchup shaped by neutral decisions. Register has reliable tools to bypass Dodge and control space, while Lucky Coward can exploit openings with swordless moves and threaten greater damage when Register's evasive options are unavailable. Both must carefully manage their cooldowns and avoid becoming predictable to maintain the advantage.

Locust Guy has no effective I-frames to counter Lucky Coward swordless moves during combos and only has R special to avoid it temporarily in neutral to gap-close against him. Lucky Coward can simply stay swordless and refuse to M1 trade to bait Locust Guy’s evasive and dodge everything he throws at him. Still, Lucky Coward needs to be extra careful as Locust Guy’s combo can consistently drain all 6 of his miracles at once, therefore, Lucky Coward needs to deal as much damage as possible outside of swordless, getting all of his miracles its a must-have before engaging against Locust Guy. This is to force Locust Guy to expend both evasive and miracle evasive from Lucky Coward before dealing stock-ending damage.

Aspiring Mangaka is a highly polarizing matchup for Lucky Coward, with the advantage shifting significantly depending on Lucky Coward's current state. In Sword mode, Lucky Coward is heavily pressured by Aspiring Mangakas' R special, which can force unfavorable M1 trades. Conversely, Lucky Coward has limited options against Swordless Lucky Coward in neutral without risking giving him Miracles through Dodge. In combos, Despair and both of Shut Up! variants are guaranteed to be punished by High Time. Lucky Coward can also quickly offhand to Swordless moves to avoid unfavorable M1 trades or Sacrilege forced by Aspiring Mangaka' R special, although this becomes increasingly predictable over time. Lucky Coward's damage output is significantly reduced by Shut Up! and Eye Catching, which can deny Backstab M1 resets, discourage Aerial Ambush in neutral, and limit the effectiveness of Cheap Shot and Dirty Play outside of combos. Consequently, the matchup tends to be slower and more patient than Lucky Coward's usual pressure game. Aspiring Mangaka needs to exhaust Lucky Coward's swordless options to secure chip damage while baiting Dodge after using R special. Meanwhile, Lucky Coward must prioritize Miracle farming to maintain a safety net before looking for damage. Neither character can comfortably impose their entire gameplan without accounting for the other's tools. But, Lucky Coward is always be able regain advantage via Swordless mode, which Aspiring Mangaka has unreliable counterplay to.

Black Death has an extremely favorable matchup against Lucky Coward, particularly while he is swordless. Injury makes evasive usage in Sword mode inconsistent and can quickly drain Miracles in neutral, preventing Lucky Coward from relying on the 1-Miracle evasive tech when comboed to 0 HP, further exacerbating his already low health. Flying Roach Swarm can avoid Ankle Cutter and High Time through its verticality and startup, then immediately close the gap against Swordless Lucky Coward. R Roach Swarm is also an oppressive dash bait that keeps him outside Black Death's side-dash range. Since it is an explosion-type attack and cannot be dodged, it discourages Lucky Coward from using Trip for Miracle generation or combo conversions. Detach is an unpunishable neutral poke that can take away a significant portion of Lucky Coward's health if Black Death wins the ensuing okizeme interactions. Its fast launch also makes confirming Taunts difficult, even with proper setup, while dodging the second Detach is highly inconsistent and often unreactable compared to blocking. Furthermore, both Festering Strikes and Chokehold are immune to Lucky Coward's swordless moves, limiting his ability to interrupt Black Death in neutral or during combos. Earthen Insect Trance's blindness, especially after blocking the second Detach, further compromises Lucky Coward's ability to use Dodge, Trip, and Taunt effectively. Overall, Black Death heavily suppresses Swordless Lucky Coward's neutral and resource generation, forcing him to rely on stronger fundamentals in Sword mode to find openings. This is especially difficult against a character capable of rapidly draining his Miracles and exploiting his low health.

Upon using Jawbreaker, the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] takes multiple steps back, winding itself up for devastating strike aimed at the target jaw. When hit, the target is locked in a short cutscene before getting ragdolled far away, getting the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbroken[/color] effect for around ~8 seconds. If whiffed, the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] come to a halt, while Lucky Coward get refunded 65% of his Awakening

When a target is suffering from the effect inflicted by the move, All of their Dashes, ability to M1 and use Skill, and sprinting are disabled. They can only walk or use their Awakening. For Lucky Coward, he heal 25 health upon landing it, and every hit done by Lucky Coward on the target is considered an interruption, granting him 1 [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Miracle[/color] every single hit

[color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] possesses two glaring flaws that will prevent optimal use of this Ultimate: - [b]Activation conditions[/b] - [b]Knockback on hit[/b] About the first: - [b]Activation[/b]: 1. The [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] must be dropped. Taken for granted. 2. Upon pressing G, the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] will reel back before charging forward. 3. Then it leaps. The [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] will trace a short path midair before: - 3.1 (if the enemy has been targeted by the sword with R special) changing course to target the nearby enemy; - 3.2 (if the sword hasn't been given a specific target) maintain its course and attempt to land at any enemy in its path. 4. Even then, the enemy must not be in [b]grounded ragdoll[/b] by the time the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] leaps. 5. Jawbreaker successfully strikes. - Strategies for [b]Activation[/b]: [b]NOTE:[/b] Now that, as of 1.78, its healing factor has been transferred to on-hit properties rather than whiff, Lucky Coward has no gain from using [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] outside as a last resort get-off-me button. 1. Be aware of when Lucky Coward can activate [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] defensively: lead the opponent into a situation where Lucky Coward can confirm it, such as endlag or active frames of a move, where the opponent is unable to dash away. 2. Set up [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] to attack offensively: while [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color], indeed, does not hit grounded ragdoll, it is perfectly capable of hitting an [b]aerial ragdoll[/b]. Lucky Coward has two tools to bring any ragdoll into a brief aerial state: [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color], and [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color]. Timing one of these two on a ragdoll the exact moment the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Hand Sword[/color] begins its leap [b]will confirm[/b] [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color]. [b]NOTE: the direction from which Lucky Coward launches the ragdoll will also be the direction of[/b] [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color][b]'s knockback.[/b] - Speaking of [b]Knockback[/b]: [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbreaker[/color] will knock the enemy far away on hit. By the time Lucky Coward gets within range of attacking the stunned opponent, the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbroken[/color] stun will be already half-expired. This is disastrous for the damage output. Lucky Coward, though, is able to deal with this within two main contexts: [b]Near a wall:[/b] 1. The first strategy in mitigating the knockback and immediately priming Lucky Coward to make full use of the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbroken[/color] stun is to, in fact, use [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color]/[color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color] to direct the [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Jawbroken[/color] opponent towards a wall to prematurely stop their travel. [b]In the open fields:[/b] 2. Fortunately, Lucky Coward's tools that aid him in confirming Jawbreaker offensively will also help him with cancelling its knockback. Indeed, timing [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color]/[color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color] with the moment the enemy is knocked away, easily told by the sound cue, will cancel Jawbreaker's knockback by replacing it with [color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Trip[/color]/[color=hsl(272, 43%, 64%)]Shoot[/color]'s own.

At an introductory stage, M1 trading consists of using the fundamentals repetitively to try an eventually breach your opponents' block. Like established in the afformentioned introduction, different characters will have different advantages and disadvantages in M1 trading, with the most important thing being finesse, how well you can jump and dash around to eventually get your opponent to face the wrong direction, at the wrong time, for you to land a crucial attack.

We already talked about the kinds of character's involved. Now we are going to talk about the options within M1 trading that people tend to do. After a player blocks, they have a few options that they can choose to do. Block -> X -> Block Value M1 Fast and Effective M1 M1 The most common path Wait, M1 The wait can throw people off Side Dash M1 Good Quick Thing Side Dash M1 M1 Also good Wait, Side Dash M1 Very good for throwing people off Headjump M1 The first time in a fight, this almost 100% works These are only some examples of what can be done. Usually, everyone has a few specific pattern they stick to. We talked about how M1 trading is all about adaption, and this is where it truly shines. You must be able to understand the patterns of your opponent, and leverage them to punish them.

There are five kinds of levels to M1 trading. Level Kills M1 / Side Dash Blocking 1 0-500 Simple M1 String. Does not turn around/predict. 2 500-1k M1 once or twice. Very minimal prediction. 3 1k-3k Incorporates Side Dashing. Turns Around 4 3k-6.5k Headjump + Delayed Side Dash Fast Prediction and Risktaking 5 10k+ Leverages an assortment of techniques to penetrate block. Actively adapts and pays attention to opponent. Obviously these are not set in stone, but the kinds of techniques that an opponent leverages tells you a lot about how good they are as a player, and allows you to learn about them on the technical scale, leading me to Adaption.

M1 trading is the core staple of JJS combat, operating as the most crucial factor in determining who is objectively 'better'. It is the most important skill to build, and oftentimes, is the key deciding factor of battles, regardless of who is using which character (with the sole exception of Disaster Plants, who operates outside of JJS's usual M1 trading mechanics). In the practical sense, M1 trading is extremely simple. It is arguably a state beyond neutral, and before combos. It is the moment that both users are directly engaging with one anothers using M1s, Dashes, and most importantly, [color=hsl(100, 100%, 75%)]Blocking[/color]. At higher states and levels of the game, these exchanges tend to last for longer amounts of time, and winning them requires Adaption. Adaption in this case, is memorizing and understanding the patterns and tendencies of opponents, how they react, M1-Dash patterns, blocking directions, and infinite other factors which contribute to the rigor of M1 trading as a whole. You will have the question; "how do I improve at M1 trading?". The key answer, and probably the answer to all of your functional mechanical/intellectual problems in life, is for you to simply practice. M1 trade with others, pay attention to your mistakes, and also the other parties' mistakes. Mechanics Involved

Seperates a good M1 trader from a God Level Goated M1 trader. Adaptation is concept about how attentive you are to the patterns of your opponent. Here is a scenario examples: "What? He got past my block by delaying his M1s and the side dashing? I'll keep that in mind." Next Encounter: "He delayed his M1, and I punished that. Now he will have to concieve another method to fight me."

Perfection can adapt to situations with his R special by changing his M1s, dashes, moves and ult moves. While not being weak, Perfection still lacks some better neutral and, comparing his combo damage to other characters, Perfection gets the shorter end of the stick. Perfection benefits the most from his flexibility and versatility, having an option for nearly every situation while still being partially an M1 merchant (who isn't?). His R special still gives him some variety by giving the player three different modes of M1s to choose from. He can outshine others by adapting to the current situation and always have an option. Also, he can make an army out of transfigured humans.

[b]All-Rounding:[/b] If you don't use your R special and stay in your normal mode, then the character works the best as an M1 merchant. If use your special once and use the Blade Mode you will lose some damage for more combo potential and a dash that can catch players off guard. If you use your special twice and use the Club Mode then you will deal shorter but high damage combos that will use less moves. Once you master the dash and the M1 trading, you'll be a monster. [b]Neutral:[/b] Stockpile (Aerial) and Focus Strike (Timed) are block bypasses that have fast startup, making it good for neutral but having high endlag on whiff. Body Repel has a [i][i]long[/i][/i] start up but is a nice ranged attack that is hard to dodge because of its aimability. It is also a gap closer and a general mobility option with its 4 + 3 variant.
Due to switching after an M1 is blocked its possible to switch from the 2nd Blade M1 to deliver a block breaking 3rd Club M1
Wherever a Downslam may be fitted in a Combo theres a high chance it could be replaced for a Club Downslam for 1-2 additional damage

One of Perfection's most reliable combo extenders. Stockpile is true and safe off any M1 string, regardless of mode. Perfection can do 3 M1s > [i]Stockpile[/i] > Any move Stockpile's 2nd swing will always connect to opponents hit by the 1st swing, allowing Perfection to turn their camera and change the direction of its knockback. This behavior does not apply when the 1st swing is blocked. Stockpile's aerial ragdoll is safe from evasives, and can function as solid evasive bait if Perfection plays their cards correctly. Relying on this isn't recommended, but can work against most opponents. Take note of the opponent's evasive habits. When timed correctly after an uppercut, the first swing can connect with ragdolls. This can be safely done on opponents without evasive for extra damage. Stockpile's second swing can be used on ragdolls to confirm a Body Repel, but otherwise it's generally recommended to use its air variant. Never do this when the opponent has their evasive. The aerial ragdoll of Stockpile launches opponents high enough to land an air M1 or Focus Strike's standard variant. Ragdoll lasts long enough to land a downslam. Stockpile's highly telegraphed startup means that using it on a ragdolled opponent, grounded or not, will likely lead to an evasive punish.

Being a block bypassing move, Stockpile can be used to win M1 trades similarly to [url=https://dogslamloop.com/characters/Honored_one/index.html]Honored One[/url]'s Rapid Punches. Be wary of spacing when attempting this, as opponents close enough to Perfection are able to block the 1st swing and interrupt them with an M1 before the 2nd swing lands. Be wary of counters for the same reason. If the opponent has their sidedash available, they may be able to dash around Perfection or out of Stockpile's range entirely before the 2nd swing connects. This can result in a punish, given Stockpile's high endlag. Stockpile's surprisingly high range can catch opponents off guard, but relying on its range too much will often get Perfection punished.

Soul Fire un-like Stockpile may be punished if used after 3M1s Due to its longer range Soul Fire may be used after a back dash or moves with high knockback to lower the risk of the combo or to tag on damage after a traditional combo ender Soul Fire's ragdoll hitting properties and long range mean it can combo of any move with more stun than its startup Soul Fires noticeable startup and non ignorable block endlag means it is punishable when used from closer ranges on non true ragdolls If used while outside of the range of a side dash + M1 it may be used to bait evasive though poorly

Being a decently fast ranged move Soul Fire may substitute a side dash + M1 punish while either of those options aren't available Soul Fires long range and semi-fast startup may be used to cancel Specials or Moves usually used outside of side dash range like the Specials of Black Death or True Cannon

Focus Strike (Standard) remembers the users M1 string and further more sets it to the 4th M1 if hit while the users M1 string is on cooldown this allows it to be used mid m1 string to slot in 10 extra damage with no cons or after an uppercut to allow for another 4th M1 most easily followed up by a downslam but can be followed up but all 3 4th M1 variants Focus Strike (Standard) hitting air ragdolls still dose its usual 10 damage but with the added benefit of less knockback than the Timed variant allowing for some added combo paths or easier execution of existing ones for the price of only 2 damage Focus Strike (Standard) is best used before doing a 4th m1 with evasive in play as its startup is noticeable and it has a high block endlag and as a rule of thumb in most places an M1 would hit Focus Strike Could work Focus Strike (Timed) unlike its sister variant always ragdols and its hit endlag is punishable in exchange this vairant dose 2 more damage and hits ragdolls while acting as a suitable combo ender Focus Strike (Timed) because of it being unsafe from m1s and the higher damage output of every other move in Perfection's aresnal of Focus Strike variants this specific variant isn't recommended to be used in combos and is usually used only for the blockbreak

The timed variant of Focus Strike being a blockbreak means it can be used to win M1 trades like stockpile however its faster startup and range mean it its above average at this though its hit endlag may cause a punish so it isn't advisable to use it in a scenario with evasive in play where Stockpile would be better used Having more range than an M1 could help out in certain scenarios but it is advised not to be used for that as the Timed variant is slightly punishable on hit and the Standard variant is slow and has noticable block endlag and whiff endlag

Both the Standard and Timed variant of Focus Strike has a special finisher If the Standard variant of focus strike finishes an opponent the opponent will burst into 1-2 Transfigured Human items at random which may be picked up and stored using the r special for later use If the Timed variant of focus strike finishes an opponent it will create 1-2 noticeably less versatile Transfigured Flesh items this finisher however is still useful because of the Standard variants inability to hit grounded ragdolls

Perfection's special, Self Transfiguration, is a mode swap (like Lucky Coward's Helping Hand), meaning it serves to change fundamental mechanics of the character or their skills. In this case, Self Transfiguration transitions the player through 3 modes. The standard order is: Fist Blade Club fist Each of the modes works as follows:
Standard 3-3-4-4 M1 string Standard Chase (Honored One, Vessel, etc.) Access to base Focus Strike and its timed variant
Faster 2-2-3-3 Blade M1 string Teleporting Chase (Similar to Salaryman's Blunt Cut) Access to Chainwhip
Slower 4-4-5-5 Club M1 string with 50% damage through block on the 1st and 2nd M1 and block bypassing on the 3rd and 4th M1 Slower, block bypassing Chase Access to Homerun

Perfection has the ability to switch modes in neutral with no restrictions other than an approximate 1/3rd of a second for the switch to happen. Thus, Perfection may use this to his advantage. For example: Switching from Fist to Blade then instantly using Chainwhip to catch the opponent off guard Switching from Fist to Blade mode then using the Blade Chase to catch the opponent off guard or punish an endlag Switching from Fist to Blade in an M1 trade when side dash goes off cooldown to prepare a faster side dash M1 Switching from Fist to Blade on the 3rd Fist M1 for a faster downslam Switching From Blade to Club mode on the 2nd or 3rd M1 to utilize the Club M1's block bypass Switching from Blade to Club then side dashing followed up by a Chase to catch opponents off guard Switching from Club to Fist to catch the opponent with a Chase or punish endlag using it Switching from Club to Fist on the 3rd Club M1 for a faster downslam

Puppet Master can be simplified as a pressure cooker, in which his kit revolves around swarming the opponent with his puppets. His unique [color=#4dd2ff]Offload[/color] special allows him to have variants on 3(basically 4) of his base moves and a new move without consuming the move's cooldown and remaining safe. Both Puppet Barrage and Offloaded Ultra Cannon are pressure tools that force opponents to block. Offloaded Ultra Spin and Heat Emission are both neutral tools that can force an opening for a combo, while all other moves like Boost On can be used at any point in a combo to extend. Using the special while it's still on cooldown will instead use [color=#c3063c]Übercharge[/color]. Puppet Master can still use his offloaded moves except Puppet Barrage in this state, but the move will be put on cooldown upon use while requiring 10% of his ultimate bar to use. While this drains a lot of ultimate bar and removes some of his tools for pressure, this can also reward Puppet Master with higher damage in his comboes. Overall, Puppet Master is a very strong character with an abundance of tools at his disposal for any given scenario in a fight. With enough range and safety from his moves, he is one of the top characters in Jujutsu Shenanigans, and will be hard to fight against if even a single hit lands.

Puppet Master general strategy is to use his moves and special to swarm and overload the opponent with pressure in different ways, whether that's to use certain moves to close in for M1s, punishing mistakes, or to keep an opponent at bay with range. If played properly, the opponent is at a disadvantage due to dealing with the threats of both the Puppet Master and the puppets, allowing for easier conversions into comboes. During the start of a game, the first goal is to get around 20-30% of your ultimate bar so you can comfortably start doing the techs Puppet Master has. This can be adjusted higher depending per player.

Use Heat Emission (non use twice) after they've wasted side dash (its both uncounterable and unblockable). Do Offloaded Ultra Spin into front dash after they've wasted side dash if your 4 isn't up or you wanna save it, they're forced to pick which one they wanna block. Both Puppet Barrage and Offloaded Ultra Cannon apply crazy pressure and forces them to block, basically free m1s if they don't track you well enough. Boost On can surprise people during M1 trades if you do M1 > Boost On instead of M1 x2, but don't expect this to work more than once or twice on competent players. Offloaded Ultra Spin is also a very useful interruption tool to punish opponents who don't bother to block it after they evasive or try to attempt their combo on the player.

Puppet Master can get a free combo off of basically any stray hit, so you're better off freestyling in all honesty. Puppet Master can land an uppercut after Offloaded Ultra Spin, so he can sneak some of those in for an extra 4 damage after Offloaded Ultra Spin. These require a bit more effort to do compared to the combo in general strategy, tends to use at least one tech listed in the Tech section. (will be moved to the combo section at a later date)

Use it combined with [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] during neutral to catch people off guard (granted this eats up your cd) Use this after 3 m1s into an [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] for safety if they have evasive up Uppercut into [i]Ultra Spin[/i] combined with an [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] or another move.

Uppercut into [i]Ultra Spin[/i] combined with an [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] is also decent for evasive baiting as they're likely not expecting the puppet and get hit by it when they attempt to punish you (R1 has a diabolical hitbox). I wouldn't recommend doing this against someone competent though. You can combo extend using this move with anything that sends them into the air (uppercut, R1, R4, very rarely R3) or on wakeup with [i]Boost On[/i] (i wouldn't recommend this tho)

You can use this during neutral to either force out a side dash or block while you do literally anything else. You can follow it up with front dash, side dash [i]Boost On[/i], [i]Heat Emission[/i], or even side dash M1. You can do [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] after an uppercut or 3 m1s into literally any move, though generally speaking you'll follow up with [i]Ultra Spin[/i] into another [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] followed up by anything. Using [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] after [i]Ultra Spin[/i], [i]Boost On[/i], [i]Ultra Cannon[/i], or [i]Offloaded Ultra Cannon[/i] is an effective way to combo extend with [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i].

Using [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] after [i]Boost On[/i] is an effective way to evasive bait as they're forced to eat at least 21.5 damage otherwise if they don't. You can do 3 M1s > [i]Ultra Spin[/i] > Delayed [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] to bait evasive as well. If ever you happen to lose an engagement, if you used [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] before you got hit then they'll automatically lose the engagement if they aren't fast enough to block it while still M1ing you or use a move that gives them some form of iframes.

This move is true and unpunishable after an M1. You can do 3 M1s > [i]Boost On[/i] > [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] to bait out evasive easily. This move can be used when the opponent is ragdolled; be warned though, as this is VERY punishable. If they don't have a counter, you can try timing it right as they get up so they can't react and evasive. Due to it's reactable windup, this is mostly used for combo filler

You side dash, therefore you [i]Boost On[/i]... In all seriousness, despite the move mostly being combo filler, you can use use it with [i]Puppet Barrage[/i] as it forces them to block. Competent players are likely to learn from this and just side dash/front dash away from you before blocking though. You can cheese M1 trades with this similar to how you would use Honored One [i]Rapid Punches[/i] in an M1 trade. Since you're considered airborne at the end of this move, you're vulnerable to both Head of Hei's Decisive Strikes and Defense Attorney's Grapple if they immediately evasive. While you can block Decisive Strikes, you can't with Defense Attorney's Grapple. Make sure you use this move while the Defense Attorney's Justice Served/evasive is on cooldown, as Grapple is a true ragdoll and can start Defense Attorney's pressure. warning!!

This move is strictly combo filler; you can't start a combo with it outside of with [i]Offloaded Ultra Spin[/i] because it's best used at range, and it's 360 blockable. It can, and mostly is used to stall for cooldowns during a combo, or to do a quick burst of damage quickly when combined with [color=#d11010] Uberstacking[/color] (refer to the [color=hsl(39, 100%, 50%)]Techs[/color] and [color=#ff0000]Combos[/color] section of [url=https://dogslamloop.com/characters/Puppet_master/index.html] Overview & Strategy[/url])

Although reacting to [i]Ultra Cannon[/i] by itself is rather simple, pairing it with an [i]Offloaded Ultra Cannon[/i] can create a mixup opportunity where players usually block the first shot but not the follow up from the cannon puppet. You can evasive bait with this move to a certain extent by holding it down and cancelling it right before it becomes charged to fool them into thinking you're leaving yourself open to being punished, albeit this is quite risky. I recommend doing this from a safe distance.

Nothing much to say here, this move is strictly combo filler, similarly to Ultra Cannon. You're mainly gonna use this move to stall for a cooldown or simply to squeeze in more damage at the end of a combo. You can use this move after Uppercut, any variant of Ultra Spin, and Offloaded Heat Emission. Aside from that, you can use Offloaded Ultra Spin, any variant of Heat Emission, and Puppet Barrage.

This move, unlike [i]Ultra Cannon[/i], is NOT strictly combo filler; it has a surprising amount of value both in combos and in neutral without any of the risks [i]Ultra Cannon[/i] has. It can be used as an area denial tool when used or to force out a block in neutral similarly to [i]Puppet Barrage[/i], which leaves them open for side dash > [i]Boost On[/i] or just pressing [i]Heat Emission[/i]. Singlehandedly THE BEST move to apply [color=#d11010]Uberstacking[/color] (as usual, refer to [color=hsl(39, 100%, 50%)]Techs[/color] and [color=#ff0000]Combos[/color] in [url=https://dogslamloop.com/characters/Puppet_master/index.html]Overviews & Strategy[/url]) by far. You go from doing a mere 7 damage to 14, not including if you use it with [i]Ultra Cannon[/i].

You can evasive bait with this move simply by placing it down and aiming it at them. If they refuse to evasive, you can shoot the cannon or save it for a later combo/attempt to evasive bait again the next time you catch them. If they try to go after the puppet and take their eyes off of you, you can punish them easily assuming you aren't too far away. Do keep in mind that they may be given burst if they hit the puppet before you can hit them.

This move is your main tool for neutral. This move is both unblockable AND uncounterable due to being classified as an explosion move. Although I did say this move is your main tool for neutral, NEVER throw it out randomly without at least wasting their side dash or forcing out a block with one of your other offloaded moves unless you're sure they can't react. It's just barely dodgable with side dash if you throw it out raw. You can use this move before or after any other move during combos, there is no move this cannot combo into, as long as you aren't too close. Your minimum distance to hit this move is side dash range.

You can use this move after M1ing the air two times and follow up with an uppercut as they're falling down, although I only recommend doing this over Heat Emission if you want to follow up with [i]Charged Ultra Cannon[/i]. You can use also use this over [i]Heat Emission[/i] if you cannot get into it's effective range in time. Just like [i]Heat Emission[/i], there is no move this cannot combo into, save for [i]Charged Ultra Cannon[/i] if you refrain from doing the uppercut follow-up mentioned above. You can catch characters during their movement abilities such as Yuji's feints if they're close enough, giving you an opportunity to punish them easily.

Quite frankly, there really isn't much to say about this move. it's almost strictly combo filler; you are NEVER starting a combo with this move unless they're stupid enough to get hit by it during neutral or it drifts behind their block. This move is mainly used to stall for cooldowns during a combo, just like [i]Ultra Cannon[/i]. Although unlike [i]Ultra Cannon[/i], it does a surprisingly high amount of damage. You can do an M1 reset with this move, albeit this requires destruction. I recommend just M1ing the air twice and then hitting the enemy with your 3rd and 4th M1 after they get thrown to avoid blue sparks.

You can use this move outside of it's intended purpose by surfing on it's head after using it. You can stack this move with [i]Heat Emission[/i] to make [i]Heat Emission's[/i] neutral even more annoying. Puppet Master general strategy is to use his moves and special to swarm and overload the opponent with pressure in different ways, whether that's to use certain moves to close in for M1s, punishing mistakes, or to keep an opponent at bay with range. If played properly, the opponent is at a disadvantage due to dealing with the threats of both the Puppet Master and the puppets, allowing for easier conversions into comboes. During the start of a game, the first goal is to get around 20-30% of your ultimate bar so you can comfortably start doing the techs Puppet Master has. This can be adjusted higher depending per player.

Use Heat Emission (non use twice) after they've wasted side dash (its both uncounterable and unblockable). Do Offloaded Ultra Spin into front dash after they've wasted side dash if your 4 isn't up or you wanna save it, they're forced to pick which one they wanna block. Both Puppet Barrage and Offloaded Ultra Cannon apply crazy pressure and forces them to block, basically free m1s if they don't track you well enough. Boost On can surprise people during M1 trades if you do M1 > Boost On instead of M1 x2, but don't expect this to work more than once or twice on competent players. Offloaded Ultra Spin is also a very useful interruption tool to punish opponents who don't bother to block it after they evasive or try to attempt their combo on the player.

Honored One's Limitless special can't consistently punish moves like Boost On or a successful Puppet Barrage, which leaves the Gojo with no other options other than to occasionally use their teleport to quickly close the distance against the Puppet Master. On the other hand, the Mechamaru player has a big advantage due to Gojo having subpar mobility, allowing the puppets to have their maximum pressure potential.

Be wary of Gojo's Limitless cooldown during neutral. Use whatever tools you have at your disposal to constantly keep advantage. Stay within your effective range and play how you like to play. For as long as you don't screw up in some certain scenarios, this matchup is an easy win due to the Gojo needing to close the distance.
How should you approach this matchup?

Vessel's quick and agile mobility allows him to quickly close the distance between him and the Puppet Master. While he is an M1 Merchant at his core, it doesn't necessarily constitute that the matchup will be easier, as Mechamaru is at his weakest when forced to M1 trade. Cursed Strikes and Crushing Blow also has i-frames during the move, making Puppet Barrage during M1 trades far less effective. Other than his mobility and i-frames though, he doesn't have anything else that can counter Mechamaru, with his counter being far less effective against the puppets and Heat Emission.

Generally, Yuji's strategy is to use his mobility to quickly close the distance and force M1 trades, so playing passive and going for punishes will be optimal. During neutral, make good use of the offloaded variants of his moves as well as base Heat Emission, as his counter targets the puppet instead of the Mechamaru, or won't trigger on Heat Emission as it is considered to be an "explosion" attack. Fully capitalize out of any hit you can get. Mechamaru's combos are especially effective at getting low HP characters near to death's door in just one encounter. Play smart with your cooldowns, you want to continuously swarm the Yuji with pressure at the right moments (e.g, when they're about to close the distance and intiate an M1 trade).
How should you approach this matchup?

Restless Gambler has no effective mobility to quickly close the distance and use his kit, making him a victim to puppet abuse. His counter also doesn't do much, only being viable in M1 trading scenarios to avoid a losing trade. Hakari's Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant is also far less effective against Puppet Master, as it doesn't actually stop any puppets that have spawned. It can stop a base Heat Emission, but at max height it just goes under. It's also harder to react to Heat Emission by responding with a projectile move, making it completely unviable to do in the first place.

Abuse your puppets. Hakari completely lacks the mobility to deal with simultaneous threats, and also lacks the effective range to have any counterplay against a Mechamaru that sits within front dash range. Just play well and cautious, a Hakari genuinely can't do anything if the Mechamaru plays good or for punish.
How should you approach this matchup?

The matchup against Ten Shadows constantly shifts, but it still mostly favors Puppet Master. Mechamaru has more tools that can be useful in niche scenarios, which does make him have the edge over Megumi. Don't let that fool you though, Megumi does have a few ways to get some counterplay against Mechamaru. Notably, Divine Dog can track and interrupt Heat Emission if used during startup. Megumi also has good mobility with his R special, which can be used to approach along with Rabbit Escape, or to escape moves like Puppet Barrage. However, Rabbit Escape is less effective against a Mechamaru, simply because it doesn't actually stop the Mechamaru player from using offloaded moves, nor does it restrict his movement (e.g, Heat Emission bypasses Rabbit Escape's restricted movement).

Be cautious over Megumi's R special. A good Megumi will use it to approach you while you have your guard down. Use Heat Emission more conservatively when they have Divine Dog out. Only use it when you are certain they can't react to the startup frame of Heat Emission or escape from it. Ultra Spin, Heat Emission, and all offloaded variants can all be used during Rabbit Escape. At best, you can convert, at worst the Megumi doesn't get their combo. Play a bit more safely, reckless skill usage will get you punished one way or another.
How should you approach this matchup?

Perfection shares a pretty similar issue with Restless Gambler, in which he struggles to approach the Puppet Master due to the lack of mobility and range. Other than Mahito's low damage Soul Fire or Blade Dash, both of which can be mitigated easily, there is nothing stopping the Mechamaru from steamrolling on the Mahito player.

Abuse your puppets. Mahito is at a constant disadvantage since they don't have any other defensive option like counters. Stay cautious. Even though it's practically "unloseable", Mahito can still deal a good chunk of your hp in his combos.

Blood Manipulator's Supernova is unfortunately not good enough to be able to have any sort of advantage outside of combos. Puppet Master's effective range far exceeds that of Choso's, meanwhile he has no good mobility option as well. Simply put, Choso's kit doesn't pair up well against Mechamaru.

The only real threat is Choso's Supernova, which you can easily subdue by abusing your effective range which still keeps you safe from Choso's general neutral range. You should also take advantage of Choso's orbless state, because the only thing that saves him from going into extreme advantage is Supernova. Punish Choso with your puppets if the Choso ever tries to camp at their FRS orb. It's either they're forced to get out, or they get into a combo.
How should I approach this matchup?

Switcher's quirky Boogie Woogie special can create some counterplay against a Puppet Master as he can either swap with the puppet or swap the Mechamaru with the puppet to easily get within close quarters and M1 trade. Despite this though, it's still not enough of an advantage for Todo to have any real advanatage against a Mechamaru, as the Mechamaru can easily use the swap against the Todo to start their own combo. Todo also loses to any other aspect, as he has terrible neutral, no good options to poke the Mechamaru, and no good way to deal with puppets other than swap.

Be wary of Todo's swaps, as he could easily use your puppets to get you into a combo. You can use moves like Offloaded Ultra Cannon so the Todo targets the puppet instead of you during neutral. Because the Todo expected to swap with you instead of the puppet, they don't expect to be right on your M1 range, which lets you win the engagement easily. Likewise, you can also use Offloaded Heat Emission and then forward dash if you know they're gonna swap with you. Once the Todo swaps with you, they immediately get caught by the Offloaded Heat Emission, to which you can convert from there. Once you shut down his swaps, it's a pretty smooth sail, as Todo is just another generic M1 merchant.
How should you approach this matchup?

Defense Attorney is another quirky matchup, to where Puppet Master still has an edge over. The main counterplay Higuruma has against Mechamaru is his RR and 3R, both of which can quickly close the distance at mid-range to force Mechamaru into a close quarters fight. Mechamaru has more tools at his disposal against a Higuruma, which does give him an advantage, though the encounters will mostly be focused on close quarters combat.

Be far more conservative with your puppets. It's best to save your puppets during CQC as Higuruma is vulnerable to interrupts during his moves. Play defensive for a while and wait for an opportunity to punish, Higuruma can easily be punished if they don't get a guard break correctly. Higuruma's R throw doesn't actually kill Mechamaru's puppets, so it is safe to set up R3 for future application in a combo.
How should I approach this matchup?

Locust Guy, another M1 merchant that can fall victim to puppet abuse! Ko-guy is THE definition of an M1 merchant, as he has no neutral options whatsoever. Puppet Master can abuse this completely and just use puppets to pressure at a distance and go in when an opportunity to convert shows itself.
